faqs.question: What does Halloween literally mean?
faqs.answer: It means "All Saints' evening". The word shortens All-Hallow-even: hallow is an old noun for a saint, and even, clipped to e'en, means evening, so it names the night of 31 October before All Saints' Day on 1 November.

faqs.question: What does the "hallow" in Halloween mean?
faqs.answer: Hallow here is a noun meaning a saint or holy person, from Old English hālga. Etymonline notes the noun is obsolete except inside Halloween, so All Hallows simply means all the saints.

faqs.question: What does the e'en in Hallowe'en stand for?
faqs.answer: E'en is a shortened "even", the older form of "eve", meaning the evening before a feast. The apostrophe marks the dropped v, which is why it sits after the e: Hallowe'en, never Hallow'een.

faqs.question: Does Halloween mean holy evening?
faqs.answer: Not quite. The hallow in Halloween is a person, the saints, so the literal sense is the evening of all the saints. "Holy evening" mixes it up with the adjective hallowed, as in hallowed ground.

faqs.question: What does Samhain mean, and how do you pronounce it?
faqs.answer: In Old Irish, samain names 1 November and the festival held on it, and in modern Irish Samhain is the month of November. Medieval scholars glossed it "end of summer", one theory among several. It is said roughly SOW-in.

faqs.question: Does Halloween mean devil's night?
faqs.answer: No. Nothing in the word refers to the devil; it comes from the saints' calendar. Devil's Night is a separate regional US name, used especially in Michigan, for pranks on the night of 30 October.

faqs.question: Is it spelled Halloween or Hallowe'en?
faqs.answer: Both are correct, but Halloween is the standard modern spelling. In our Google Books Ngram query, Hallowe'en was still the majority British spelling as late as 1992 and fell to 11.6% of uses in 2015 to 2019; in American books it is 1.8%.

faqs.question: What is Halloween called in Irish?
faqs.answer: Oíche Shamhna, literally "Samhain night", which Ó Dónaill's Irish-English dictionary gives as the Irish for Hallowe'en. Scottish Gaelic uses the matching Oidhche Shamhna.

faqs.question: What is the difference between All Hallows' Eve, All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day?
faqs.answer: All Hallows' Eve is 31 October, the evening Halloween is named after. All Saints' Day, or All Hallows' Day, is 1 November, honouring the saints, and All Souls' Day on 2 November is for praying for all the dead.

faqs.question: What is Auld Hallowe'en?
faqs.answer: Auld Hallowe'en is the Scots name for Halloween kept on 11 November under the Old Style calendar, recorded in the Scottish National Dictionary. It is the same festival counted on the older calendar's date.

# What Does Halloween Mean? The Word Explained, Root by Root

What does Halloween mean? It means "the evening of All Hallows", the night before All Saints' Day on 1 November. "Hallow" is an old English noun for a saint, and "e'en" is a clipped "even", meaning evening, so the word literally says *All Saints' evening*.

[Etymonline's entry for Halloween](https://www.etymonline.com/word/Halloween) dates "alle halwe eue" to about 1300 and the Scottish short form to the 1560s. On the calendar it means 31 October: Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027.

We build one-person greeting pages at SubhSandesh, where 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone and 90.9% of started pages get published and sent, so the answer sits first and fits one screen. Below: each part of the word, its dates, related terms, five languages, the myths and the spelling.

## What does the word Halloween mean, piece by piece?

Halloween is a compound worn down over seven centuries. It is All + Hallow + e'en, and each piece meant something first.

### Hallow: a saint, not just "holy"

In Old English, *hālga* was a noun for a holy person or saint, and Etymonline notes that this noun is now obsolete except inside Halloween. The verb "to hallow", to make holy, survives in "hallowed ground", which is why so many people read the word as "holy evening". Strictly, All Hallows means all the saints together.

### E'en: evening, shortened twice

"Even" is the older form of "eve", the evening before a feast, as in Christmas Eve. Scots speech clipped it to "e'en", and the apostrophe marks the lost "v". The [Scottish National Dictionary entry for Hallow](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd/hallow_n2) defines Halloween as the eve of All Saints' Day, 31 October, and records the spoken form *hallaleen* in Angus, Edinburgh and Dumfriesshire as recently as the 2000s.

### How to spell it: Halloween or Hallowe'en?

Quick answer: write **Halloween**; both spellings are correct, but the apostrophe is now a deliberate, old-fashioned choice. We queried Google Books Ngram data on 13 October 2026: in [British English books](https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=Halloween%2CHallowe%27en&year_start=1800&year_end=2019&corpus=en-GB-2019&smoothing=0), Hallowe'en was still the majority spelling as late as 1992, then fell to 11.6% of uses in 2015 to 2019. In American books it last led in 1946 and now sits at 1.8%.

- Use "Halloween" for general writing and anything you want found in search.
- Use "Hallowe'en" on a vintage-style card or when quoting an older text.
- Never write "Hallow'een": the apostrophe stands in for the v of "even", so it goes after the e.

## When was the word Halloween first recorded?

Most explainers disagree on the date because they are dating different words. The full phrase came first, the Scots contraction centuries later, and the modern spelling only won in the 20th century.

- **c. 1300:** "alle halwe eue" names 31 October (Etymonline).
- **Mid-1400s:** "All Hallowen" or "Allhallowe'en" for the evening before All-Hallows (Etymonline).
- **1560s:** the shortened word in a Scottish context (Etymonline).
- **1621:** Alexander Montgomerie's *Flyting* is printed with "Alhallow euen", a night when elves and the King of Fairy ride out.
- **1745:** the oldest quotation in the Scottish National Dictionary, which only covers 1700 onwards: a letter planning a few days away "to keep our halyeen".
- **1785 to 1786:** Robert Burns writes his poem "Halloween". Etymonline dates it 1785 and credits it with popularising the word; the dictionary quotes the 1786 printing.

So the often repeated "first used in 1745" is half right. That is the Scots dictionary's oldest quotation, spelled *halyeen*, but Etymonline traces the short form nearly two centuries earlier.

## Related words: All Hallows, All Souls, Allhallowtide and Samhain

Halloween belongs to a cluster of calendar words, and its neighbours explain it. The table gives each one's literal sense and the earliest date we could confirm in a dictionary we opened.

| Term | Literal meaning | Language or origin | First attested |
|---|---|---|---|
| Halloween (Hallowe'en) | All Saints' evening | Scots shortening of All-Hallow-even | 1560s (Etymonline); Scots dictionary's oldest quote 1745, as *halyeen* |
| All Hallows' Eve | Evening before the feast of all the saints | Middle English *alle halwe eue* | c. 1300 (Etymonline) |
| Hallowtide, later Allhallowtide | The season around All Hallows | English *hallow* + *tide*, "time" | Hallowtide 15th century (Etymonline); Allhallowtide not verified |
| Samhain (Old Irish *samain*) | 1 November and its festival; medieval scholars glossed it "end of summer" | Irish | Not verified |

Only the English forms carry firm dates. We could not confirm Samhain's earliest record in an open dictionary, so we leave it blank.

All Saints' Day, also called All Hallows' Day, is 1 November, the feast the eve belongs to. All Souls' Day follows on 2 November, for praying for all the dead. Church calendars group the three days, 31 October to 2 November, as Allhallowtide.

Scotland kept extra words. The same dictionary lists *Hallowday* for 1 November, *Hallowmas*, a *Hallow-fair* market, and **Auld Hallowe'en**, kept on 11 November under the Old Style calendar. In Ulster it records *Halloweve* or *Haleve*, with one 1930 source saying Halloween was "never being used except in educated circles".

In Old Irish, *samain* names the first of November and the festival held on it, and in religious texts it means All Saints' Day, according to the [Electronic Dictionary of the Irish Language](https://dil.ie/36129). The popular gloss "summer's end" comes from medieval Irish scholars who split the word as *sam-fuin*, the ending of summer; modern linguists treat that as one theory among several. In modern Irish, Samhain is simply the month of November in [Ó Dónaill's Irish-English dictionary](https://www.teanglann.ie/en/fgb/Samhain), and it is said roughly "SOW-in", never "sam-hane".

## What does Halloween mean in other languages?

Many languages never translate "Halloween". They name the saints' feast or the season, or borrow the English word:

- **Irish and Scottish Gaelic: Oíche Shamhna and Oidhche Shamhna**, "Samhain night"; Ó Dónaill gives Oíche Shamhna as the Irish for Hallowe'en.
- **Welsh: Nos Galan Gaeaf**, "the night of the calends of winter"; Calan Gaeaf, 1 November, is All Saints' Day.
- **German: Allerheiligen**, "of all saints", a word-for-word copy of Latin *omnium sanctorum*, naming 1 November itself.
- **Serbian: Ноћ вештица (Noć veštica)**, "night of the witches", as used in the Serbian summary of the 2025 folklore paper below.
- **Japanese: ハロウィン (harowin)**, a straight loanword; the JMdict dictionary also lists ハロウィーン.

## What Halloween means to people today

The same date now carries several meanings at once. Folklorist Christopher Heppa's fieldwork paper [Halloween in Britain: Then and Now (Folkloristika, 2025)](http://doi.fil.bg.ac.rs/volume.php?pt=journals&issue=folk-2025-10-2&i=9) shows how quickly the balance moved in one country. He interviewed a small set of people between January and April 2025, so it is evidence of change, not a measurement.

- **Religious:** for many Christians, 31 October is still the vigil of All Saints, followed by prayers for the dead on 2 November.
- **Community and secular:** dressing up, carving and knocking on doors. Interviewed in 2025, a 93-year-old woman from Crewe answered "Nothing!" when asked what she did for Halloween as a child in the 1930s, and folklorist Steve Roud described a north-south line in England, with little done in the south.
- **Commercial:** Heppa credits the films *Halloween* (1978) and *E.T.* (1982) with making British children want to trick-or-treat; costumes, sweets and pumpkins followed, and pumpkins replaced turnips as lanterns.
- **Children:** apple bobbing and turnip lanterns in Heppa's 1950s Cheshire; costumes and sweets now.
- **Opting out:** some families and churches skip it for reasons of faith, and that is a meaning too.

## Common misconceptions about what Halloween means

Most myths about the word come from guessing at its sound rather than its history. Four are worth correcting.

- **"Halloween means holy evening."** Close, but the hallow is a person, the saints. "Holy evening" blurs the old noun into the adjective "hallowed".
- **"Halloween means devil's night."** No part of the word refers to the devil. *Devil's Night* is a separate regional US name, used especially around Michigan, for the night of 30 October when young people play pranks; parts of the UK and New Jersey call that night *Mischief Night*.
- **"Samhain was the Celtic god of the dead."** In the Old Irish dictionary *samain* is a date and a festival, never a deity.
- **"The name proves Halloween is pagan."** The name is wholly Christian, taken from the saints' calendar. Heppa reports that the folklorists Iona and Peter Opie wrote in 1959 that Halloween was never associated with paganism, despite strong popular belief; how far Gaelic seasonal customs fed into the night is still disputed among historians.

## Sending the meaning to one person

Knowing the night belongs to the saints and the souls can change what you send. A churchgoing grandparent may prefer a gentle note on 1 or 2 November; a friend who loves the spooky side wants the 31st.

For that friend, the [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) is built for one recipient: you add their name and yours, a letter, up to six photos and a word to carve on the pumpkin. They knock three times on a small haunted house, catch falling sweets, carve the jack-o'-lantern until your word glows, and read your letter by flashlight.

For a word-lover, carve "e'en" and put this page's one-line meaning in the letter. The closing question, "Will you be my boo?" by default, changes with the partner, bestie, family or kids mode, and the kids tone has no blood, gore or jump scares. It ends with a 1080×1920 Boo License reading "Valid every 31 October, forever".

To explain in your own voice, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice note of up to 60 seconds and a letter of up to 3,000 characters. Timing matters less than people fear: at Raksha Bandhan 2026, the nearest festival we have measured (89 pages), 49.4% of greeting pages were built on the day itself.

### When a greeting page is the wrong tool

For a class, a parish group or a party, a greeting page is the wrong choice: it speaks to one person, not a crowd, and its interface is English only. Someone who wants the full etymology is better served by a dictionary link, and on a phone screen a long letter tires the reader.

## Sources

- Etymonline, "Halloween" and "hallow" (undated, revised continuously).
- Scottish National Dictionary, "Hallow, n. 2" (1960; 2005 supplement).
- Electronic Dictionary of the Irish Language, "samain" (undated).
- Ó Dónaill, Foclóir Gaeilge–Béarla, "Samhain" (1977).
- Heppa, "Halloween in Britain: Then and Now", Folkloristika 10/2 (2025).
- Google Books Ngram, Halloween vs Hallowe'en, 2019 corpora, queried 13 October 2026.

structuralLimitations: Brief framing 'earliest attested use c. 1745 Scottish' is only half right: 1745 is the Scottish National Dictionary's oldest quotation (form 'halyeen'), and SND covers 1700 onward only. 'Hallowe'en is still used in UK/Canada': UK verified only as a minority form in books (11.6% in 2015–2019). Canada not measured; the Ngram has no Canadian corpus, so the body makes no Canada claim.
